📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Remarked It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

It has been revealed that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

In a recent development, each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

Industry observers note that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

According to recent reports, we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Sources indicate that table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

According to recent reports, training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

Industry observers note that in a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

Industry observers note that in our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

Industry observers note that and bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

It has been revealed that if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 indicates which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

Industry observers note that the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

According to recent reports, table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

In a recent development, the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

It has been revealed that figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

In a recent development, table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Sources indicate that figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

It has been revealed that the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

In a recent development, the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

Sources indicate that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

It has been revealed that figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Sources indicate that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Industry observers note that training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Industry observers note that zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

Industry observers note that no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

It has been revealed that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

In a recent development, the question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

It has been revealed that we used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

According to recent reports, each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Recent findings suggest that figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

Industry observers note that we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

It has been revealed that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

It has been revealed that when sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

Industry observers note that when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In a recent development, in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

According to recent reports, we release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:.

The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation.

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Danny, Amit, Yotam, Tamar, Yonatan and their teams are joining forces to build a complete security platform for the age of AI.

Danny, Amit, Yotam, Tamar, Yonatan and their teams are joining forces to build a complete security platform for the age of AI.

Recent findings suggest that in 2021, before Oasis Security was even founded, I sat down with co-founder Danny Brickman and came away thinking he had something familiar. He demonstrated the same drive weâd seen in the founders of two other Sequoia companies, Wiz and Cyera, whose founders, like Danny, had come up through Talpiot, the leadership program of the IDF. I wrote about that meeting a couple of years later in my investment memo, when we backed Oasis Security, at the Series A. I didnât realize at the time how literally connected that comparison would turn out to be. Today, Oasis is joining Cyera â and it turns out the foundersâ stories make the case for this combination almost as well as the technology does.

According to recent reports, three years ago, the pitch for Oasis was simple: enterprises were about to have far more machine identities than human ones, and almost nobody had a real way to manage or secure them. That was true then. Itâs far more true now. Every AI agent creates or uses non-human identities â API keys, service accounts, OAuth tokens, agent-to-agent credentials â that act with real permissions and real blast radius, and that donât behave anything like the human identities the last generation of identity tooling was built around. AI drove non-human identity from a niche IAM subcategory to a board-level CISO conversation. Danny Brickman and his co-founder Amit Zimerman built Oasis, which they call agentic access management, for exactly that world.

Cyera arrived at the same shift from a different direction. Yotam Segev, Tamar Bar-Ilan, and Yonatan Itai built the company to answer a deceptively simple question: where does an organizationâs sensitive data actually live, who can reach it, and whatâs really at risk? As AI agents started reading, writing and acting on that data, they reached a conclusion that now looks obvious: securing AI means securing the data, the identities acting on it (human and non-human), and the agents themselves.

Sources indicate that put the two products side by side, and they complement each other perfectly. Cyera knows where the sensitive data is. Oasis knows who or what can actually touch it â every service account, API key and agent credential, and whether itâs behaving the way it should. Itâs a bit like a bank vault: the best way to protect it is by knowing both whatâs inside and whoâs approaching. Data security tells you whatâs actually at stake. Identity security tells you whether the thing touching your data is legitimate. Together, the two products cover the entire path an AI agent takes through a companyâs environment, from the data it touches to the identity it uses to touch it.

Thereâs a practical case here too. Cyera has built one of the most powerful enterprise GTM teams, with the kind of scale that usually takes a startup a decade to reach. Oasisâs product now gets to run through that engine, into enterprise accounts it would otherwise have taken years to earn on its own. And the market isnât waiting: Whoever builds the first genuinely complete AI security platform, spanning data, identity and agents, has a real shot at becoming the default layer enterprises standardize on as agentic AI rolls out. Speed and completeness both matter, and the combination of Cyera and Oasis creates both.

In a recent development, the foundersâ backgrounds make the fit feel almost inevitable in hindsight. Itâs a small world: two teams weâd backed independently, drawn from the same pool of Israeli technical talent, ended up building the two halves of the same answer to AI security. Talpiot and Unit 8200 alumni have produced a disproportionate share of the last decadeâs major cybersecurity companies, so the coincidence is smaller than it looks, but itâs still a good sign when it plays out this cleanly.

Danny, Amit and the Oasis team built the category-defining firm in non-human identity in under three years, from a standing start to a product enterprises trust with agentic access at scale. That doesnât happen without genuinely hard technical work, and a founder team that saw the shift to agentic AI before almost anyone else in security did. We at Sequoia have backed both Cyera and Oasis since their Series A rounds, and weâre proud to keep backing this team as they take on the next chapter together â a bigger stage, and an opportunity sized to match.

  • The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • Sources indicate that the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

Sources indicate that the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

According to recent reports, to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We proposal to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

It has been revealed that select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script debuts its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

Sources indicate that A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

In a recent development, each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel blueprint use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS states nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space highlights comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Recent findings suggest that each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alon and team are training a foundation model for defensive cybersecurity, for enterprises to defend themselves against AIâs scaling offensive capabilities.

Alon and team are training a foundation model for defensive cybersecurity, for enterprises to defend themselves against AIâs scaling offensive capabilities.

Cybersecurity is a perpetual fight between the good guys and the bad. The age of agentic AI and Mythos-class models has tipped the scales in favor of the bad guys, opening a Pandoraâs box for offensive capabilities. An explosion in CVEs has since ensued.

Industry observers note that cyberattacks are about technical exploitation, which requires coding and reasoning prowess. Anthropicâs Mythos can discover and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities. Any model paired with a harness brings the cost of social engineering attacks down to near zero, unleashing them at unprecedented scale. The danger is heightened with every newly introduced model release.

Defensive security isnât improving in parallel. The relevant data lives in logs, events, traces and telemetry, a fundamentally different modality than the bodies of text LLMs usually train on, which barely show up in pretraining. Unlike offensive cybersecurity, which involves goal-directed reasoning towards a defined objective, defense requires open-ended reasoning, continually finding anomalies across vast amounts of normal-looking activity, a distinct capability that typically demands extensive domain-specific training. In short, defense is out of distribution for general-purpose frontier models: neither the data nor the intuition it requires is well-represented in training. In the race toward AGI, we cannot expect the frontier labs to take the detour of overhauling their training pipelines for defensive cybersecurity. And we certainly canât afford to bet our security on a hope that they do.

It has been revealed that corma has illustrated this âdefense gapâ in testing. They ran red/blue team simulations where an attacker plants a hidden backdoor and a defender tries to find it. The defender failed to find the backdoor 78% of the time, even when the defender was an identical copy of the very same model that planted it. Holding model quality constant, attackers will always have an advantage.

The only answer to scaling laws on offense is better scaling laws on defense. Recent events have shown that frontier AI for defensive cybersecurity is one of the crucial unsolved problems of the AI age. Solving it is the generational mission Corma was founded on.

Sources indicate that corma founder and CEO Alon Pluda and his team are training a foundation model to power defensive cybersecurity agents. Cybersecurity, like Go or chess, is a two-player, zero-sum game with a clean reward (were you breached or not?) and an endless supply of games to play. Reinforcement learning and self-play have produced superhuman results before in this kind of paradigm. We are seeing history repeat itself. Corma pushes this further with large-scale reinforcement learning across cybersecurity environments that replicate real enterprise networks, with all their tools, telemetry and noise â as part of a training pipeline that produces frontier defensive capabilities, outperforming general-purpose foundation models, with much lower per-token inference costs.

In the cat-and-mouse game of cybersecurity, we believe Cormaâs vertical integration and âsovereign AIâ approach will win. Cost matters (always-on inference costs can rack up quickly). Owning the model weights matters (they arenât subject to restrictions on cybersecurity-related usage set by the closed model labs). And specialization and inference speed really matter (fastest to protect against a fresh threat wins).

Cormaâs foundation model is deployed and productized as an agentic Security Workforce. These workers operate across different security tools and take on roles spanning the entire security organization: from security operations and identity management to cloud and network security and beyond. They are on the job at Fortune 500 companies and large enterprises across healthcare, finance, critical infrastructure, retail and more.

In a recent development, cormaâs foundation model powers agents that complete defensive work end to end. We spoke to one CISO whose Corma agent notified him of a pending attack through his Garmin watch while he was on a walk with his dog in the evening; with one confirmation, the agent was able to shut the attacker down, all while he was still walking. In another instance, within its first hour on the job, Corma uncovered, contained and remediated an active attacker campaign inside a customerâs network that their security team had missed for 52 days.

Sources indicate that training frontier foundation models for defensive cybersecurity requires world-class hackers and world-class researchers â almost no organization on earth has both. Alon is personally one of the most elite hackers in the world, and has assembled a cohesive and interdisciplinary team of hackers and researchers that is hill-climbing on technical challenges and building impressive commercial momentum.

We are thrilled to lead Cormaâs seed round and to be their partner as they chart new territory in what is sure to be one of the most dynamic races in AI.

#216. Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (871 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Capillus HairBand Review: Good Looks, Awkward Fit

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird.
  • Recent findings suggest that discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side.
  • According to recent reports, interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Excepting the few models that look like regular hats, most red-light therapy for hair growth devices look … well, pretty weird. From stormtrooper helmets to headpieces that look like they were designed for Geordi La Forge, these aren’t exactly accessories you’d want to wear in public. Which is why it was nice to unbox the Capillus HairBand and find, at long last, a normal-looking headband.

Recent findings suggest that discreet black, fabric-covered, and sized like a normal hair accessory, the HairBand’s only indication it might do something more than hold back hair is a little 2 x 1-inch battery pack that sits jauntily cocked to one side. It’s refreshing to finally see a red-light device that doesn’t embarrass the user or frighten animals and young children, but after testing it for over a month, I found the HairBand has its share of shortcomings for the price.

According to recent reports, interestingly, Capillus makes a series of full-coverage devices with laser diodes built into what looks like a normal black baseball cap. However, the cheapest of these hats runs $1,699, and the most expensive “triple-wavelength” model, with 312 laser diodes, runs $3,299. The 2-inch-wide Capillus HairBand provides a similar laser diode treatment for less, at $599 with only 82 diodes (650 nm). (Capillus notes the headband is designed to prioritize areas where hair loss is most noticeable, such as the hairline and temples.).

Sources indicate that unlike straight LED lights, laser diodes provide collimated beams of light that travel in a straight line, allowing for more focused and intense treatment of hair follicles. I actually saw some success with this treatment when I tested the HairBand’s closest competitor, Hairmax’s LaserBand 82 ComfortFlex ($849). It couldn’t help follicles that were scarred or had already died, but studies have shown that red-light therapy can energize follicles that have more recently become dormant.

I did see some growth in the middle of my part with the LaserBand, and while I stopped using it to switch to the HairBand exclusively for the past five or so weeks, I admit this growth did make it difficult to isolate the HairBand’s contribution, especially since the headband’s coverage area is so small. Thus, the following observations are mainly on the wearing experience of the HairBand, not hair growth.

It has been revealed that at only 2 inches wide and five minutes per section, the HairBand took at least 15 minutes to cover my entire part, compared with the 3-inch-wide LaserBand, which also only needs to be used three times per week at 30 seconds per section for a total of 90 seconds. I’m a Type-A full-time working parent in my mid-forties, and let me tell you—15 minutes of doing nothing is a long time in my world.

Recent findings suggest that the HairBand has teeth and could sit on my head as long as it was in a normal headband position, right in the middle, but the weight of the battery pack pulls it forward ever so slightly, so if I was leaning over or doing anything that didn’t hold my head exactly straight, it would start to slip off. This meant I had to hold it with my hand, which meant no multitasking.

Capillus’ marketing materials use words like “ritual” and feature pictures of twentysomethings admiring themselves in the mirror, but I can’t imagine these women are suffering from the perimenopausal hair loss that would necessitate use of a red-light device in the first place.

According to recent reports, I don’t consider myself to have an overly large head and have never had trouble with hats or other hair accessories, but this headband, which weighs only 6 ounces, felt quite small and somewhat precarious on my head overall. I should note it is also rather overtly feminine in style—my husband and I were able to share “custody” of the LaserBand, but he declined to wear this one, and I didn’t blame him.

There were two other concerns during my testing. One, the back of the box stated it contained quick-start instructions, but my box only had the headband and USB-C charging cord—no physical user guide to be found (except online, but I had to do some googling). Not that one is needed, since it’s pretty obvious how it works—push the start button on the battery pack, and it will beep and shut off when the five minutes are up—but it’s an odd omission at this price point.

Recent findings suggest that two, this device is not presently FDA-cleared for treating hair loss or promoting regrowth. This isn’t ideal, but FDA-cleared is much different from FDA-approved; it simply requires the manufacturer to prove its product is “substantially equivalent” to an already FDA-cleared product. (And it doesn’t ensure results, just that it’s safe to use as directed.) Capillus’ rep tells me the brand is currently working on the FDA filing for the HairBand, which was released in September of this year, and intends to have it cleared in 2027. (The brand’s cap-style devices are FDA-cleared.) Even so, the HairBand is a unique device in this space, but if I’m spending that much on a red-light device, I would prefer a little more versatility in the design.

Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LFM3 is our upcoming generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • According to recent reports, LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM3 is our upcoming generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

According to recent reports, LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

In a recent development, the payoff reveals at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:.

In a recent development, each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Recent findings suggest that reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

According to recent reports, for brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

We can't wait to see what you build.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stefan and Veljko are building the AI-native workspace for quality video creation.

Stefan and Veljko are building the AI-native workspace for quality video creation.

Thereâs something magical about watching a developer in flow state, fingers flying as they type into Codex, Claude, or Cursor. A powerful creation interface unfolds in response to every keystroke, powering a workflow that would have been unrecognizable, even alien-like, to any professional software engineer just two years ago. The entire IDE has been torn down and rebuilt from scratch for the age of AI, and developers are flying as a result.

Sources indicate that video models have raced ahead over the same two years. Yet unlike coding, video creation remains stuck in the stone age, with its entire toolchain still built around capturing, uploading, storing, and editing enormous files.

In a recent development, generative video is at a threshold moment: the models are now expressive enough to become the upcoming camera. The bottleneck is no longer the technical art of animation or the $100M budgets for film crews and visual effects; itâs human creativity and token inference. But video creators are not yet flying.

Without a proper AI-native tool suite, or a âCursor for video,â the people who make films, TV series, and commercials for a living remain stuck bolting model outputs onto legacy editing pipelines. Generation, review, and production tracking each live in a separate application; workflows buckle under the sheer volume of material; and a finished take often canât be traced back to its source for legal clearance. Itâs a gaping problem and is the biggest roadblock on the industryâs path to truly embracing AI.

Preview clears that block. An AI-native video creation and production platform built for professional creators, Preview combines a video timeline with an infinite canvas for ideation into one collaborative multiplayer workspace. Teams can generate with any model and track every character, location, and prop, with complete records of how every asset was made. It enables both halves of a hybrid production to work together seamlessly. There is simply nothing like it in the market.

Co-founders Stefan Fejes and Veljko Tornjanski have been best friends since high school in Serbia, and were seemingly born for this mission. They were founding team members at video creation pioneer Veed; later, at Vizcom, Veljko was the first hire and became Head of AI, while Stefan led Product. They understand well the tricky nuances of video, they have deep empathy for their customers, and they have delivered sophisticated, polished work on impressively short timelines.

More than 100 studios are already actively using Preview, from agencies making commercials for Fortune 500 brands to AI-native studios to Hollywood feature filmmakers. Simply put, they love it. Customers tell us it has become the most significant tool in their work, and the single source of truth from which all downstream inference flows.

We are at the precipice of a video token tsunami, and many billions of dollars of inference will run through this category, driving the next wave of iconic films and IP. Value will accrue to where the work actually happensâthe platform a creative team opens in the morning and closes at night, where the decisions get made and the record gets kept. We believe Preview is that platform, and that this is the right team, the right product, and the right moment. We are thrilled to partner with Stefan and Veljko and to lead their seed round.

#206. Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds

📅 23 Mar 2026 • ⏱️ 29m • 📚 Deep Dive (5713 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds

📅 23 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 29 min read (5713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~29 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year.
  • For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops.
  • Updated November 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations to include the new PROLED MacBook Pro that I recently reviewed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year. Not all are winners, and many should be avoided, no matter how slick the marketing or how cheap the discount. Good news: It’s my job to recommend laptops that fit your budget and won’t make you regret your purchase six months later. These are my favorite laptops that I’ve tested myself and would highly recommend you buy.

For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops. My guide on How to Choose a Laptop may also help if you’re undecided.

Updated November 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations to include the new PROLED MacBook Pro that I recently reviewed. I’ve also adjusted my picks throughout and checked prices.

When friends or family ask what laptop to buy, I always start with the MacBook Air. It is far more powerful than its compact size suggests. It’s a shame about the recent $200 price increase from $1,099 to $1,299, but even at that upcoming price, it remains my top pick because it nails the substantial picture. Everything from the trackpad to the speakers is of the highest quality, and it delivers all the performance and battery life the average person needs.

With the latest M5 chip, its GPU matches the M3 Pro MacBook Pro, easily handling everything from gaming to video editing. That’s not at all what the MacBook Air is designed for, but the performance is there when you want to dabble. It’s what makes it feel like a do-it-all machine, all contained in a fanless chassis that’s still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. Oh, and did I mention it’ll last well over a full workday away from the wall socket and perform just as well on battery as when plugged in? In almost every aspect, it’s the gold standard.

In a recent development, while the lower price of the latest MacBook Neo might be tempting, the MacBook Air is the better choice for anyone working at a computer all day. With its superior performance, extra memory, faster storage, and Thunderbolt ports, you will never have to question if you have the right tool for the job. (And unless you already know you need a MacBook Pro, you probably don’t.).

It has been revealed that speaking of price, I have to mention the upcoming Dell XPS 13 next. I like just about everything about this laptop, whether it’s the compact size, the excellent build quality, or the gorgeous screen. It’s not OLED, but it’s sharp, bright, and color-accurate. It also includes a 120-Hz refresh rate, which makes animation and motion on the device look super smooth. The XPS 13 is filled with features like that, which don’t normally end up in a laptop at this price. While it doesn’t have what I’d call powerhouse performance, the Intel Wildcat Lake chip inside gets the job done for basic, day-to-day computing tasks. That translates to great, all-day battery life, competitive with the MacBook Air. Just don’t try to play games, edit high-resolution video, or take it to engineering school.

The XPS 13 is especially good for those who want a compact device to travel with. With its tiny bezels, it’s still one of the best laptops to use on a plane. But even beyond that, it’s just one of the best laptops you can buy under $1,000 right now. The Dell XPS 13 is primarily being talked about as a budget laptop, thanks to its $700 starting configuration. But that model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which limited performance in my testing. You’ll probably just want to avoid that 8 GB model. Most people will want the upgraded 16 GB model, which you can get for $900. It’s the best hardware you can buy for under $1,000.

It has been revealed that if you want a Windows laptop that still feels high-end but has a bit more performance, I would point you to the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. It might be the prettiest Windows laptop you can buy right now. The device is beautifully built and incredibly sturdy, with a thin chassis, an oversized haptic trackpad, and polished metal edges. I also appreciate the three Thunderbolt 4 ports split between both sides for convenient charging, as well as the surprisingly good speakers. I tested the high-end model, which features a fast Snapdragon X2 Elite, 32 GB of RAM, and a gorgeous 2880 x 1800 OLED display. The screen offers near-perfect colors, excellent brightness, and astounding HDR performance. It doesn’t get much better than this. It’s usually quite expensive, but we’re finally seeing discounts that bring it to a more reasonable price. There’s also an Intel model with a very efficient, powerful chip that would be a good choice. I’d go with whichever is cheaper right now.

And lastly, for something with a larger screen, I’d recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It’s a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with a 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and a 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000 on sale at Amazon. While it’s slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports, including HDMI, USB-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided. Lenovo also sells a cheaper version directly, but it has a lower-resolution IPS screen that I haven’t tested. The $30 it costs to upgrade the display to a higher-resolution OLED is well worth it.

While “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but HP always has some version of the OmniBook 5 with a Snapdragon CPU for around $700 or so. The specific discounted configuration seems to change every few days, though, so shop carefully. I’ll be testing the latest model soon, which switches to Intel processors and starts at $699.

I also recently tested the latest HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for under $550. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.

According to recent reports, the MacBook Neo is Apple’s new entry-level laptop. It launched at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently risen to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly prioritized the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a far better choice for remote workers—the Neo is an extremely premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual owners. Thanks to the lower-powered A18 Pro chip, though, performance does take a hit. So, be careful about buying this laptop if you work on a computer all day.

Sources indicate that given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. Perhaps that’s why Google introduced the next evolution of the platform, so to speak: the Googlebook. The first batch has been released into the world, and I’ve tested a number of them. Googlebooks are similar to Chromebooks in use case, but they run entirely on Android and include some exclusive Google Gemini features. I like the close integration with Android, but Googlebooks ended up being a bit of a letdown, mostly because they’re so expensive. The Acer Googlebook 14 and Dell XPS Googlebook are the two standouts in my book, as both use a Snapdragon X-series chip to deliver really great battery life. The XPS Googlebook is particularly pretty, with a chassis nearly identical to the XPS 13. But $999 is a tough price to swallow. It ultimately has some of the same limitations as Chromebooks: you can’t download applications from the web and must rely on the Google Play Store. The Acer Googlebook 14 is probably my top pick, as it’s the cheapest at $899. Even that isn’t exactly what I’d call a “budget laptop,” though.

It has been revealed that that’s why I strongly recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514, especially when it’s on sale for under $700 (which happens often). It uses an efficient (and responsive) MediaTek Kompanio Ultra that delivers excellent battery life. For most people, I wouldn’t recommend spending over $500 on a Chromebook; if you’re paying more, consider the MacBook Neo or the HP OmniBooks, which offer more than a Chromebook’s limited scope. But the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 might be the best combination of display, touchpad, and battery life at this price, making it a good choice for the right person—so long as you know what you’re paying for.

According to recent reports, truly cheap Chromebooks come with bigger compromises, especially in display quality, touchpad feel, and battery life. If you really need something dirt cheap as a starter laptop for a kid or as a secondary device, I’d recommend the Asus Chromebook CX14. It has a modern design, enough ports, a good keyboard, and decent storage.

The laptops above are great for most people, but content creators and gamers need extra performance. No option is better than the new OLED (or PROLED, as Apple calls it) MacBook Pro. No laptop feels more premium than the MacBook Pro, combining incredible performance with the brightest OLED screen ever put in a laptop. The brightness levels have never been seen on an OLED laptop before, making this the dream machine for producing and consuming HDR content. Regardless of what you’re doing, you’ll certainly notice the difference. It’s also the first MacBook Pro to get a touchscreen, a long-awaited feature.

Industry observers note that I should mention, though, that it doesn’t take a step forward in terms of performance. For the first time since this generation of MacBook Pro launched in 2021, it uses the same M5 Pro or M5 Max internally. With rumors that the M6 Pro and M6 Max are being skipped entirely, you’ll have to accept that you’re paying a lot more for the same performance. To make the decision harder, Apple still sells the previous-gen model—so you’ll have to decide whether the upgraded screen is worth the $400 extra. For my money, it totally is.

Meanwhile, Windows has made its first successful attempt to properly compete with the MacBook Pro. I’m talking primarily about the launch of Nvidia’s newly introduced RTX Spark “superchip” and the new laptops that use it. To be clear, despite Nvidia’s involvement, these aren’t gaming laptops. Like the MacBook Pro, they’re designed first and foremost for running heavier creative applications and on-device AI. The Surface Laptop Ultra is a great example, which has a lot in common with the standard 15-inch Surface Laptop. But the differences internally are substantial. The Surface Laptop Ultra uses a single chip that integrates the CPU, GPU, and memory together, allowing up to 128 GB of memory to be shared across the system. That’s not unlike how Apple Silicon works, dramatically increasing on-device AI performance. So, if you’ve been curious about running LLMs right on your laptop without relying on the cloud, these RTX Spark laptops are a great place to start. The other two RTX Spark laptops I tested, the HP OmniBook Ultra 16 and Lenovo Pro 9n, share a lot with the Surface Laptop Ultra (including performance). The OmniBook Ultra is the thinnest of the three, but I prefer the Surface Laptop Ultra’s Mini-LED display and 3:2 aspect ratio.

Perhaps the most common use for extra laptop performance, however, is gaming. If you plan to boot up graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, I’ve come back to the Lenovo LOQ 15 as my top pick. There are cheaper RTX 5050 models, such as the Alienware 15 or MSI Cyborg A15, but prices have been increasing on these laptops over the past few months. The Alienware 15 with the RTX 5050, in particular, has seen a $600 price jump, which makes it incredibly overpriced.

That’s led me back to the LOQ 15, which has stayed steady at $1,300 at Walmart and gives you an RTX 5060 for graphics and a bright, colorful screen. You won’t find a cheaper gaming laptop that doesn’t make some significant compromises in either performance or screen quality, both of which can sour the gaming experience. And while I wish the LOQ 15 were still selling for under $1,000 as it did at launch, it’s still the best gaming laptop for the money right now. It’s really the only gaming laptop under $1,500 I’d at the moment buy, given where prices are.

In a recent development, there’s also a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, their sleek design works just as well for school or work as it does for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While you can buy more powerful options, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade. They’re expensive, but if you can afford them, they’re as premium as gaming laptops get. I’ll soon be testing the latest version of the Blade 16, which includes Intel’s upcoming Panther Lake chips and should offer vastly improved battery life.

If you choose one of the laptops above, you will be very happy with your purchase. However, if you are looking for a specific feature or a different price point, I have included a few other options below that I’ve recently reviewed and enjoyed using. Each of these recently tested laptops has at least one minor drawback, but they could still be the perfect choice depending on your needs and current discounts.

Framework Laptop 13 Pro for $1,599: We’ve always loved Framework laptops at WIRED, mainly because their internal components are so repairable and upgradable. Consumers can easily swap out nearly every part, including the CPU. The Framework Laptop 13 Pro uses the same internal structure as the basic Framework Laptop 13, but upgraded with a haptic touchpad, an aluminum chassis, and a brighter (and sharper) display. The result is the Framework Laptop I’ve always wanted, especially with an all-black aesthetic that hints at ThinkPad inspiration. But most of all, if you’re going to try and make a laptop last for many years, it makes sense that it would be something more premium. This one actually feels like it’s worth the investment.

Microsoft Surface Laptop 13.8 for $1,000: The Surface Laptop 13.8 (also known as the 7th Edition) was one of my favorite laptops throughout 2024 and 2025, primarily because of its premium build quality, great battery life, and 3:2 aspect ratio screen. And while I still love this laptop, it’s risen dramatically in price and no longer feels like a great value, especially since it’s two years old now. The 2024 model now starts at $1,200, though I’ve occasionally seen it dip under $1,000. The next-generation model with the Snapdragon X2 chips costs $1,700, but I have seen that price come down as low as $1,250 on discount.

Dell 14 Plus for $1,172: There was a time—2025, to be exact—when the Dell 14 Plus was as affordable as $600. It was easily the best deal in the world of Windows laptops, primarily because the Dell 14 Plus has a 2560 x 1600 display and a smooth touchpad—two things laptops at that price typically lack. You’re paying for the Mini-LED screen and extra ports. Unfortunately, compared to the other MacBook models, it got a $300 price bump to $1,999. On discount, you’ll often find it selling for $1,799, though, which is solid for the specs.

Sources indicate that asus Zenbook A16 for $2,200: The Zenbook A14 and A16 are Asus’ ultralight laptops, weighing just 2.16 pounds, making them some of the lightest laptops you can buy right now. This second-generation Zenbook A16 is still incredibly light and now comes with second-generation Snapdragon X2 chips. How Much Should You Spend on a Laptop?

Industry observers note that if you’re shopping for a laptop, you probably already have a budget. But some context might help put things in perspective. The cheapest laptops cost around $200, but laptop prices can range as high as $5,000. Meanwhile, the average amount people spend, according to the best data we have, is around $750. That lands decidedly in the midrange, splitting between the more expensive devices that are more than $1,000 and the budget-tier machines you find below $700.

In a recent development, when we talk about pricing, it’s often the “starting” price of the laptop, meaning the lowest-priced configuration. This is really notable to consider, as you want to compare devices apples to apples as much as possible. For example, a cheaper laptop might start at $750 with 256 GB of storage, while a more premium laptop might start at this same price but come with 512 GB or even 1 TB of storage. Increasingly, you can find some really decent laptops around this price, some of which we’ve listed.

According to recent reports, if your budget needs to be under $750, though, there are still good options. Laptops below this price tend to come with compromises. Most commonly, it’s the quality of the display and touchpad that suffers, as these are things you can’t gauge from a spec sheet or reference photo. Or it might be a performance-related matter, such as the 8 GB of memory in the MacBook Neo. If you’re shopping for something under $500, Chromebooks often give you the best bang for your buck.

So, why spend more? Well, there are two primary reasons. First, you might want a more premium design, perhaps one that has a more daring aesthetic or high-end components. Take the MacBook Pro, for example. It starts at $600 more than the MacBook Air but comes with a brighter mini-LED screen, significantly better speakers, and more ports. The second primary reason to spend more than $750 or so is to get more performance. Whether for gaming or content creation, laptops with discrete GPUs cost more, which is why it’s hard to find a worthwhile gaming laptop for less than $1,000. If you’re buying a gaming laptop, plan to spend a few hundred bucks more.

What Are the Best Laptop Brands?

Unlike the smartphone world, the biggest laptop brands have been around for more than 40 years. Besides Apple, four laptop brands stand out for adopting the latest technology and trends while providing reliable support and service.

Sources indicate that lenovo is the biggest PC brand in the world, at least in terms of global shipments. It’s perhaps most well-known for its familiar sub-brands like ThinkPad and Yoga, but it also isn’t afraid to take risks with more experimental designs and advanced technology. Lenovo has also made a name for itself in the gaming space with its Legion laptops, known for balancing performance and features at competitive prices.

Asus has promptly become a favorite, notable for the sheer number of laptops available in the consumer market. The tech giant takes a similar approach to Lenovo, which has led Asus to innovate quickly on new technology and designs while also launching premium laptops at more affordable prices than its competitors. Gaming, in particular, is a space Asus has come to dominate, with the ROG Zephyrus, Strix, and TUF brands leading the way.

Sources indicate that dell and HP are generally more conservative, but both have recently undergone significant rebranding. In 2024, HP replaced its Spectre and Envy lines with the OmniBook name. Meanwhile, Dell briefly retired its well-known Inspiron and XPS sub-brands in 2025, though it has since reversed course and brought the XPS line back.

Other notable laptop brands include Microsoft Surface, Samsung, Acer, LG, and MSI, though none have the same global footprint as the top four.

How Do I Choose the Right Laptop?

If none of these laptops resonate with what you’re looking for, that’s OK! There are far more laptops than we have time to test. To help you make smart choices, we put together a complete laptop buying guide. We also cover the CPUs and GPUs you need to know. We recommend sticking to these guidelines:.

According to recent reports, RAM: We recommend 16 GB of RAM. That’s become the upcoming standard, even in more affordable laptops. Upgrading to 32 GB is even better, so you won’t have to worry about running out of memory, especially if you’re a gamer or video editor. The recent memory shortage has led to some dramatic price increases, largely based on configurations of RAM. Apple’s launch of the 8 GB MacBook Neo this spring has led to the return of high-end 8-GB Windows laptops as well, such as the Dell XPS 13.

CPU: For Windows laptops, you have three CPU brands to choose from: Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm. Intel’s Core Ultra Series 2 debuted in late 2024 and delivers a huge boost to battery life. It also has the best integrated graphics of the three. Core Ultra Series 3 is just now rolling out and, based on my testing, is extremely impressive in performance and efficiency. While AMD chips are primarily used in gaming laptops, they’ve struggled to gain ground on Intel elsewhere.

In a recent development, qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, however, have seriously challenged Intel over the past year with their ARM architecture, offering some of the best battery life we’ve ever seen on Windows machines. The second generation, Snapdragon X2, was unveiled last fall and rolled out slowly throughout 2026. They improve performance, but in many cases, they've led to more expensive laptops, while previous-gen laptops are still available that cost less.

Sources indicate that starting this year, there’s also the choice of Nvidia’s new RTX Spark platform, which gives you the option of 18-core or 20-core CPUs. More on that in the GPU section below.

Apple Silicon is what powers all the modern MacBooks, the latest of which is the M5 chip. Read our in-depth guide on Which MacBook to Buy for more information.

Industry observers note that graphics: Want to play AAA PC games, edit video on your laptop, or run local AI models? You’ll want some powerful graphics on hand. At this point, Nvidia is the primary option. The RTX 5090, launched in 2025, is still the most powerful latest GPU available, but the 5040-series remains a good option.

It has been revealed that integrated graphics have improved significantly over the years, though, especially on processors made by Apple, AMD, and Intel, such as the Apple M5 or the Intel Core Ultra X9 388H. Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform uses a single “superchip” that provides unified memory to both the CPU and GPU to improve AI performance.

Industry observers note that screen: The display depends highly on the size of the laptop. A 1,200-pixel resolution (HD+) screen on a 13- or 14-inch laptop looks sharp enough to get by, but you’ll want more pixels on larger displays, such as a 2560 x 1600, 2880 x 1800, or 3840 x 2400. While IPS screens are good enough for most people, OLED and Mini-LED are becoming more common, offering better color accuracy, deeper contrast, and excellent HDR performance.

Connectivity: We generally recommend at least two USB-C ports, along with one HDMI and one USB-A port for legacy devices. (Remember that nearly all laptops today use one of those USB-C ports for the power adapter.) Thankfully, most laptops still have headphone jacks, but always check, because a few models have dropped them. Lastly, make sure it supports Wi-Fi 6E or newer. Even if you don’t have a Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 router yet, you’ll likely have one in the future (see our Best Routers or Best Mesh Systems guides if you need a new one).

In a recent development, battery life: Battery life is extremely competitive these days, with Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel all making highly ambitious battery-life claims. Most laptops with the latest chips (and without discrete graphics) will get you more than 10 hours of battery life, or many more if your workload is lighter.

Sources indicate that as mentioned, in Windows-based laptops, there are three primary options for CPUs: Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. All three companies offer good processors, but it really depends on the type of laptop. For premium laptops, you’ll want something like the Intel Core Ultra 258V or Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite. Meanwhile, for budget laptops, Snapdragon X is the best choice. And for gaming laptops, I’d recommend something from AMD, such as the Ryzen AI 9 365. All three companies have unveiled next-gen chips for 2026, and there’s some exciting stuff coming soon.

In a recent development, intel’s latest chips, known as either Core Ultra Series 3 or codename Panther Lake, are slowly rolling out in new laptops, such as the Dell XPS 14. These chips represent a massive leap forward in both CPU and integrated graphics performance. While highly impressive, they will soon face fresh competition from upcoming AMD and Qualcomm releases.

According to recent reports, qualcomm made a major impact in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips. Similar to Apple’s M-series, these ARM-based processors prioritize efficiency to drastically improve battery life. This has been a game-changer for Windows laptops across different price points. The Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite is the highest-end option for performance, but the Snapdragon X Plus and base Snapdragon X still offer equally strong battery life, despite showing up in much cheaper laptops. The sequel was unveiled in late 2025, and now in 2026, we’re seeing those laptops roll out. Unfortunately, like Intel’s latest chips, laptops with this next-gen silicon tend to be significantly more expensive than their predecessors.

AMD has grown into a competitive player in the gaming laptop space. Its latest processors, including the Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 9900X3D, are the most powerful gaming chips you can find in a laptop. Unfortunately, it’s still hard to find many laptops supporting these killer chips. AMD also offers its Ryzen AI 300 H and HX chips, which are more commonly found in gaming laptops. While they also offer a mainstream Ryzen AI 300 series, these chips aren’t found in many laptops and currently fall short of the battery life offered by Intel and Qualcomm.

Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform just hit the scene, promising to deliver power and efficiency, especially when running AI-based operations. It’s not as ubiquitous as Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm chips, but it’s something to watch for.

In a recent development, I have been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, and WIRED contributor Chris Null has been testing them for 25 years. We test each laptop we review in a variety of situations, including both synthetic benchmark tests and real-world use cases. We make comparisons against similar equipment. We don’t just look at the specs—our reviews evaluate performance, usability, portability, and price to help you find the right laptop for your needs.

We put every laptop through a gauntlet of tests before writing a review and assigning a rating.

Hands-on use: We evaluate the exterior of the device. We compare how thin and light it is against other laptops. We repeatedly open and close the lid to test the quality and ease of the hinge. We push on weak points like the keyboard and lid to test build quality. We also extensively test the keyboard and touchpad for comfort and precision. By using each laptop as our daily driver for days or even weeks, we can spot real-world quirks—like awkward port placement, excessive bloatware, or unexpected problems that may make the laptop difficult to use—that you won’t see on a spec sheet.

Sights and sounds: Once we boot up the device, it’s all about the sights and sounds. The screen is paramount, as it’s your window into everything the laptop has to offer. While you can tell a lot about brightness, color, and contrast just by looking, we go beyond subjective testing. We use a Spyder colorimeter to precisely measure brightness, contrast, color saturation, and accuracy. For HDR-capable screens, we also test peak brightness with HDR content. Finally, we evaluate the webcam and speakers to ensure they are ready for your video calls and streaming sessions.

Performance testing: Finally, we test performance. We always evaluate a laptop based on what it’s intended for—we don’t expect a $500 budget laptop to run like a gaming powerhouse, or a gaming rig to get 18 hours of battery life. Our testbed includes more than 20 synthetic benchmarks, which we constantly adapt based on the device's CPU and operating system. These include tests within Geekbench, PCMark, 3DMark, Procyon, GFXBench, Puget Bench, Superposition, Cinebench, and various gaming-related tests such as 3DMark and Cyberpunk 2077. While we don’t generally report raw scores, we pay close attention to what they tell us. We also monitor fan noise, surface temperature, and overall battery life during these tests.

It’s a lot, I know. But we’re thorough, because we want to stand by our recommendations and ensure that the laptops we rate highly are worth the money.
